title: Compassion Stories
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: The talk's main teaching is about cultivating compassion in difficult situations by acknowledging and accepting our own emotions, rather than trying to suppress or numb them. By doing so, we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and others, allowing us to connect with their suffering and respond with kindness and love. This approach is reflected in the Bodhisattva vow, which encourages us to act with compassion regardless of our circumstances, even when it feels impossible.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome.
It's nice to see everyone here.
Let's see if I have enough light.
Can you turn it up just a little bit?
Thank you.
Thanks, that's great.
We've been having some talks on compassion lately, and I'm going to talk about that tonight as well.
I thought I would tell you some compassion stories that I've come across in my reading in the last couple of years, and then a couple of compassion stories from the family that I grew up in.
I think there'll probably be a little time at the end for questions or discussion, or if anyone has a compassion story they'd like to tell.
There may be time for that too.
A few years ago I was invited to speak to the comparative religion class at Squalicum High School, and I've been going there twice a year for the last couple of years.
It's a pretty neat class.

They cover all the major religions, and the teacher has a practitioner from each religion come in to talk about their day-to-day practice, how it affects their life, and some of the basic principles of each religion.
I don't know if he asked everybody this, but he asked me to bring some compassion stories to tell.
Here are a couple of the ones that I use for the class.
The first one is from 17th century Japan, and it involves the teacher Bankai.
He lived from 1622 to 1693 and was a well-known teacher in his time.
Students from many parts of the country would come to his monastery to study.
He was leading probably a practice period, and after a couple of weeks it was reported to him that one of the monks was caught stealing.
He took that information, but he didn't do anything.
A couple of weeks later the same monk was caught stealing again, and a couple of the other monks talked to Bankai and asked him to expel the accused monk.
Again he listened to them, but he didn't do anything.
No surprise, a few weeks later the same monk was caught stealing a third time, and this time people were upset.
They called a meeting with Bankai, all the monks including the accused monk, and they said to him, "If you don't expel this monk, we are leaving.
We will go to other monasteries to study."
This is what Bankai said to them: "You may go if you wish to go, but I'm going to keep this monk here.
You are lucky monks.
You know the difference between right and wrong, but this poor monk does not.
If I don't keep him here, who's going to teach him the difference between right and wrong?"
According to the story, at that point the accused monk burst into tears and did not steal again.
With these old stories we don't really know: did this really happen, did it happen the way it's written?
But it's a vehicle for talking about how you would handle something like this.
Do you just throw the person out?
Do you try to work with them?
That's one of the compassion stories.
The next one is from 20th century America, and it involves Diane Rosetto.
She's a Zen teacher in California, now in her 70s, and she's a Dharma heir of Joko Beck.
This story is from her book *Waking Up to What You Do*, which is about the Zen precepts, and those of you who are studying for Jukai, I'm sure you're familiar with this story.
This is from her early life, long before she began a Buddhist practice.
In 1959, when Diane was a junior in high school, she got pregnant.
As usually happened back then, she dropped out of school and married the guy that got her pregnant.
A little while later they had a second child, and as usually happens when really young people have children and get married, the marriage failed.
After a few years she found herself a single parent with two children and no high school diploma, really struggling to get by.
I'm just going to quote you a few of the things that she said in the book.
*My world was pretty much limited to soap operas, washing diapers, and figuring out how I was going to pay the rent each month.
After a short period on the welfare rolls I found whatever jobs a high school dropout could get, a factory worker, a nightclub hostess, a barmaid, just to support myself and my children.
I soon figured out that prospects would be pretty dismal if I didn't get some education, so I returned to school hoping just to get my high school diploma and perhaps a decent job as a secretary.
But it didn't work out that way thanks to Mr.
Sheldon Daly, a Boston lawyer.
I lied my way into Mr.
Daly's office after I read in the newspaper's classified section that he was looking for a legal secretary to run his office.
By now I had taken the necessary courses to earn my high school certificate but my office skills were far from what the job required.
I managed to convince him that I could type and take shorthand a lot better than I demonstrated in my interview.*
Some of you may not even know what shorthand is.
You're young enough.
*I arranged for him to call for references from a friend who would back my story.
He believed me and he hired me.
And it wasn't long before it became clear to him that I was making a mess of things and that I had lied to him about my skills.
One day he sat me in his office and he said, "Look, this isn't working out.
I don't want to hear about why you misrepresented yourself when I asked for your qualifications, but what I do want to know is how would you like your life to be five years from now?
What kinds of choices do you think you need to make to make that a reality?"
The question left me dumbfounded.
Not only was he telling me to get a life, but he was also saying that I had an option to choose what my life could be.
He was more interested in how he could help me than how he could judge me.*
*Like a good Zen riddle, Mr.
Davis' question wormed its way into my psyche, forcing to the forefront of my thinking possibilities that I had only dreamed of in the past.
When I met with him again, I told him I wanted to go to college and to perhaps become a teacher.
That's all he needed to hear.
He got on the phone, he made a few phone calls, and within a few months I found myself attending night school as a college freshman.
Seven years later, my life had made a complete turnaround.
I had finished college and graduate school, married my current husband of 35 years, and was in the midst of parenting adolescence.*
So her boss could have just fired her, and most bosses probably would have, but what a life-changing thing it was for him to try to help her out.
The next story involves Joanne Cacciatore.
I came across an article about her in a Wisdom Publications catalog.
The article said that she's a Zen priest and a professor of psychology at Arizona State University.
She works in the area of traumatic loss and grief, both doing research and helping people cope with traumatic loss.
She had a baby daughter die in 1994, and that event moved her to work in this area.
Her recent book is entitled *Bearing the Unbearable*.

The article I read didn't say anything about her Zen training, and I didn't find anything online other than a mention that Thich Nhat Hanh, Joan Halifax, and Jack Kornfeld have been important influences, but there's quite a bit online about her academic work at Arizona State University.
Anyway, here's her story.
About two years ago, when she was 50, she was just starting a hike in the desert in Arizona, I assume, where she lives.
She'd been to this area 40 years before, when she was 10 years old, with her family, and had vowed to take this particular hike, but she had not had a chance to do it in 40 years.
So here she is, just started out on this hike.
She said she was three minutes into the hike on a trail when she came across a horse that had fallen down and was being beaten by its handler.
The horse was bleeding and undernourished and just lying there.
She burst into tears and got really upset, and the handler left because he didn't want to be around for her being so upset.
I'll just quote you what she said.
She said, "I sat on the ground and I went to touch his face," this is the horse, "and he closed his eyes and turned his head as if he was afraid I was going to hit him.

I started to apologize to him for what humans had done to him, and I said, 'I'm so sorry.' I felt his head lay in my lap, and he turned his head and looked at me with his incredibly deep eyes, and I saw in him myself.
Twenty-three years earlier, when my child died, I knew if I left him on the trail and didn't take action, it would be like leaving myself on that trail.
I knew that saving him was just like saving myself, and saving him was just like saving the world."
So she stayed with the horse, she got on the phone, she got authorities involved, and she had the horse transported to a vet where it stayed for a while.
Then she took the horse to her property and rehabbed it.
There's a video online where you can see the horse running around the corral, healthy and happy and living a happy life.
So that had a nice outcome to it.
But here's what she says about grief and compassion.

"I stay connected to my deep, deep trauma and pain that happened 23 years ago that has made me able to connect with the suffering of other beings in a deeper way than I ever could have when I was younger.
We grieve for that which we love, we don't grieve when we don't love.
When we disconnect from our grief, when we turn away and can't look at our grief, then it also cuts us off from love.
You can't feel the love for someone who died without also feeling the pain when they're not there.
When we create space in our hearts and minds for grief to be what it is and we have compassionate others around us for support, we can grieve and feel happy at the same time.
We can grieve and feel content and joy at the same time."
With compassion, she goes on to say, "If we all do the good we can do with what is in our range and our reach, the world would be a different place.
If we all said, 'Yes, I will make a difference with what I can.
Whatever crosses my path, I will act with compassion.'" I really like the way she describes that particular way of being compassionate.
To me, it's just like the Bodhisattva vow, a vow to save all beings.
It's impossible to do, but no matter how many times you might miss the chance to be compassionate, there will always be another chance.
There will always be something crossing your path sooner or later.
I often have trouble knowing what to do about the big problems in the world: poverty, injustice, war.
It feels like there's nothing you can do, or even if you do something, it often feels like it doesn't make a difference.
But it's good to be reminded to pay attention to what crosses our path, because something always will, sooner or later.
And keep in mind the notion of your range and your reach.
You don't have to go beyond your range.
There will always be something within your range.
So that's the compassion story from Joanne Cacciatore.
Now I'll tell you four stories from the family I grew up in.
That would be my two parents, and then I have a sister who's two years older.
When I was in high school, I was a pretty good student.
Not great, but pretty good.
I thought I wanted to go to college after high school, and I thought I knew what I wanted to study, but I was wrong on both counts.
It would have been, in hindsight, better for me to take a couple of years and work and travel and give myself a little chance to grow up and think about what I wanted to do.
But since all my friends were going to college, I didn't even consider anything else.
So I went to college.
I only looked at two places.
I think back in the 60s, people didn't look around so much for colleges.
Anyway, I didn't look around very hard.
I got in, I went, and I did well the first quarter.
Then every quarter after that, I got worse and worse.
It turns out I wasn't very interested in the stuff I was taking, and I didn't really look around for anything else.
By the spring of my sophomore year, I had flunked out.
And 1967 was a bad year to lose your student deferment.
I knew I would be going into the military.
But the worst part was having to tell my parents, because I really hadn't said much about how I was doing and they hadn't asked.
So this happened, and there was no one to blame but myself.
This was all my doing; nobody else was responsible.
This happened 50 years ago, and I'm sure I've lost some of the details, but I remember this one conversation really clearly.
I was riding with my father, who was driving.
I said, "Hey Dad, guess what?"
He said, "What?"
I said, "I flunked out of college."
There was a little pause.
He said, "Well, I flunked a few classes myself when I was in college."
I said, "Well, no, that's not it.
I flunked out.
They kicked me out."
There was a longer pause.
Then I braced myself.
He's going to be mad, he's going to be disappointed.
I was really disappointed in myself.
And I thought for sure they were going to compare me to my older sister, who was Phi Beta Kappa and getting ready to enter medical school.
But all he said was, "Well, you're going to have to figure out what you want to do now.
Let me know if I can be of any help."
And that was it.

My mother at the time, she's different now, but at the time she was pretty critical and had very definite ideas of what people ought to do and how they ought to do it, and wasn't shy about letting me and other people, mostly me, know.
But she didn't say anything at all.
I was amazed about that.
In my family, we really didn't have much.
I don't remember any conversations about life transitions, becoming a teenager and socializing.
I don't remember conversations about what you want to do in school.
We just didn't have that.
But my parents were hardworking and responsible and had good values and were kind.
I knew that they loved me and they wanted me to do well, and they expected me to handle this.
I got myself into it, and it was my thing to take care of.
So I got a job, and pretty soon after that I went in the Navy.
I had a few years there to figure out what I wanted to do, which I did figure out.
But it was very helpful that they did not add judgment and criticism, because I had plenty of it already.
They never criticized me for that, which is kind of surprising.
I think compassion includes certain actions, but it can also include not doing things.
I'm sure they must have had criticism and judgment and been upset, but they withheld it.
It helped me just do what I had to do and not have another layer to deal with.
So that's one story.
The next one happened in 1979-80.
I had been in Bellingham about a year, and I was dating someone, and then we moved in together.
We were living together, and we had an unplanned pregnancy.
I hadn't thought very much about being a parent, being a father, other than I think I'd like to have kids someday.
That's about as far as it went.
So we had to decide, what are we going to do here?
We decided, well, we'll have the child.
Then a month or two after that, she had a miscarriage.
So we decided, well, we'll just get pregnant again.
So we did.
And then about four months after that, we split up.
That was not the plan.
But it became clear pretty soon after we split up that we really weren't a good fit as a couple, and we were not going to get back together.
I don't know how I missed that earlier, but I did.
Actually it's fine, because the baby here is my daughter Gillian, and I'm very happy to have her in my life.
But we had to figure out, well, now what are we going to do?
How are we going to do this?
We would meet to talk about it, and we just ended up getting in an argument.
I felt terrible: how could I be in this situation?
I'm going to be a dad, but I'm not even married.
I'm not living with her.
I just felt like this is not a good thing.
Gillian's mom was talking about moving back to the East Coast, and I saw no way this was going to work out.
I just couldn't see anything.
I thought I'd fly to the East Coast once a year for a short visit, and that would be about it.
I'm sure it was much harder on Gillian's mother, being a single mom and being pregnant and alone.
But it was really hard for both of us.
Once Gillian was born, however, we were able to talk to each other and figure out all the things we had to figure out, sharing the parenting and money and all that stuff.
It went surprisingly well, and it's actually gone well to this day.
Through it all, again, my parents were kind and welcoming to everybody.
They welcomed Gillian as they did their other grandchildren, who came in a more traditional way.
They were kind and welcoming to Gillian's mom.
And again, no judgment toward me, which was much appreciated since I had plenty of it already.
Last summer, my mother had her 100th birthday.
I know my dad died about 15 years ago.
Everybody went down to Eugene, where she's living now: Gillian and Carolyn and I, and my sister and all her kids and their families, and also Gillian's mom and her husband.
We had a really nice time there.

Afterwards, Gillian's mom wrote a letter to my mother just saying how nice it was to see her again, and appreciating the kindness that she received from my father and my mother back then, but also through the years, and how much it meant to her and how much it still means to her.
That was really a good reminder that compassion just lasts forever.
It's kind of like love.
When you receive it, it doesn't go away.
It was really something.
Anyway, I'm pretty sure my parents must have had worry and criticism.
I never actually talked to them about it afterwards.
But they never judged me, never criticized me for those things.
So that was really something.
Anyway, I guess that's probably enough for me.
